planting.note: Plant rooted cuttings or divisions in spring into moist soil with morning sun and afternoon shade; confine the aggressive rhizomes to a buried pot or root-barrier bed.

directions: The historic commercial strain behind most American peppermint oil production, identifiable by its dark purple-flushed stems and near-black leaf veining. Mint tolerates Gulf Coast humidity far better than Mediterranean herbs do, but in zone 9a's humid summers give it morning sun with afternoon shade and consistently moist soil. Cut back hard after flowering to refresh leaf quality and oil concentration.
sources: Mountain Valley Growers - Organic Mentha piperita Peppermint Plants

planting.note: Divide and plant in spring into consistently moist soil with partial shade during Gulf Coast summer afternoons; divide every 2-3 years and confine roots to prevent spreading.

directions: A clump-forming Central Asian spearmint selection with crinkled, rounded mid-green leaves and an unusually clean, strong spearmint flavor prized for mint sauce, jelly, and iced drinks. It handles heat well but, like all spearmints, wants steady moisture and benefits from partial shade during Gulf Coast summer afternoons to keep leaves from scorching.
sources: Promesse de Fleurs - Mentha spicata Tashkent

planting.note: Divide and plant in spring into consistently moist soil in partial shade; confine roots to prevent spreading into adjacent beds.

directions: A close relative of Moroccan mint with broad, pointed, textured light-green leaves and a clean spearmint flavor well suited to sauces, vegetable dishes, and mint tisanes, closely associated with the mint traditionally used in Spanish and North African tea culture. Documentation for this cultivar is thinner than better-known spearmint selections, so verify current nursery availability before planning around it. Give it the same moist, partly shaded conditions as other spearmints.
sources: Promesse de Fleurs - Mentha spicata Spanish

planting.note: Plant rooted cuttings in raised, gritty, sharply drained soil in full sun; root rot from wet soil, not heat, is the real limiting factor on the Gulf Coast.

directions: A culinary thyme bred for ornamental gray-green foliage edged in creamy white with a burgundy winter cast, fully usable in bouquet garni, stuffings, and sauces. Like all thymes it is intolerant of wet feet, so plant in raised, gritty, sharply drained soil and resist overwatering during humid summers. Treat it as a short-lived perennial in zone 9a and take cuttings each spring as insurance against summer rot.

planting.note: Plant rooted cuttings in gritty, fast-draining soil in full sun; harvest before flowering for the strongest orange-balsam aroma.

directions: A common-thyme selection valued for orange-scented, sweeter-than-species foliage, excellent fresh or dried in fish dishes, sauces, and citrus-forward marinades. It needs the same gritty, fast-draining soil any culinary thyme requires to survive Gulf Coast humidity, since root rot rather than heat is what kills thyme in zone 9a. Shear lightly after bloom to keep the mound tight.

planting.note: Plant rooted cuttings after last frost into a raised, gritty mound in full sun; go easy on water and mulch against the stem, since culinary sage is highly prone to crown rot in Gulf Coast humidity.

directions: A dwarf common-sage selection with a short, compact habit and smaller, narrower leaves than the species, useful for containers and tight raised-bed plantings where full-size sage would sprawl. It is less broadly documented than other dwarf sage selections already in the collection, so treat it as a real but less certain distinct cultivar. Like all culinary sage it resents wet feet and heavy mulch against the crown.
